request.user:
[2024 summer phd probability — problem 2]

Part I, Problem 2. $X$ has a Geometric$(p)$ distribution if $f(x; p) = (1-p)^{x-1} p$ for $x \in \{1, 2, \dots\}$. Let $X_1, X_2$ be independent with $X_j \sim$ Geometric$(p_j)$, and $Y = X_1 + X_2$.
(a) Find the MGF of $Y$ if it exists, or verify it does not.
(b) Find the pmf of $Y$ in simple closed form.
(c) Prove or disprove: for each fixed $y \in \{1, 2, \dots\}$, the pmf $f(y; p_1, p_2)$ is continuous as $p_1 \to p_2$.

response.text:
Let \(q_j=1-p_j\), \(j=1,2\). Assume \(0<p_j<1\) unless otherwise noted; the formulas extend to \(p_j=1\) by taking \(q_j=0\).

---

## (a) MGF of \(Y=X_1+X_2\)

For a single \(X_j\sim \operatorname{Geometric}(p_j)\),

\[
M_{X_j}(t)=\mathbb E[e^{tX_j}]
=\sum_{x=1}^\infty e^{tx}q_j^{x-1}p_j
=p_j e^t \sum_{x=1}^\infty (q_j e^t)^{x-1}.
\]

This geometric series converges iff

\[
q_j e^t<1
\iff t<-\log q_j
= -\log(1-p_j).
\]

Therefore,

\[
M_{X_j}(t)=\frac{p_j e^t}{1-q_j e^t},
\qquad t<-\log q_j.
\]

Since \(X_1,X_2\) are independent,

\[
M_Y(t)=M_{X_1}(t)M_{X_2}(t).
\]

Thus

\[
\boxed{
M_Y(t)
=
\frac{p_1p_2 e^{2t}}
{\bigl(1-(1-p_1)e^t\bigr)\bigl(1-(1-p_2)e^t\bigr)}
}
\]

for

\[
\boxed{
t<\min\{-\log(1-p_1),-\log(1-p_2)\}.
}
\]

For \(t\) outside this range, at least one of the two geometric series diverges, so the MGF is not finite there. Since the range contains a neighborhood of \(0\), the MGF exists.

---

## (b) PMF of \(Y\)

For \(y\in\{1,2,\dots\}\),

\[
\mathbb P(Y=y)
=
\sum_{x=1}^{y-1}\mathbb P(X_1=x)\mathbb P(X_2=y-x).
\]

If \(y=1\), the sum is empty, so

\[
\mathbb P(Y=1)=0.
\]

For \(y\ge 2\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb P(Y=y)
&=
\sum_{x=1}^{y-1}
p_1q_1^{x-1}p_2q_2^{y-x-1} \\
&=
p_1p_2 \sum_{k=0}^{y-2} q_1^k q_2^{y-2-k}.
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(p_1\neq p_2\), equivalently \(q_1\neq q_2\), then

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{y-2} q_1^k q_2^{y-2-k}
=
\frac{q_1^{y-1}-q_2^{y-1}}{q_1-q_2}.
\]

Since \(q_1-q_2=p_2-p_1\), we get

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(Y=y)
=
\frac{p_1p_2}{p_2-p_1}
\left\{(1-p_1)^{y-1}-(1-p_2)^{y-1}\right\},
\qquad y\ge 2,\ p_1\neq p_2.
}
\]

If \(p_1=p_2=p\), then \(q_1=q_2=q=1-p\), and

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{y-2} q^k q^{y-2-k}
=
\sum_{k=0}^{y-2} q^{y-2}
=
(y-1)q^{y-2}.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\mathbb P(Y=y)
=
(y-1)p^2(1-p)^{y-2},
\qquad y\ge 2,\ p_1=p_2=p.
}
\]

Thus the pmf is

\[
\boxed{
f_Y(y;p_1,p_2)
=
\begin{cases}
0, & y=1,\\[4pt]
\dfrac{p_1p_2}{p_2-p_1}
\left\{(1-p_1)^{y-1}-(1-p_2)^{y-1}\right\},
& y\ge 2,\ p_1\neq p_2,\\[10pt]
(y-1)p^2(1-p)^{y-2},
& y\ge 2,\ p_1=p_2=p.
\end{cases}
}
\]

---

## (c) Continuity as \(p_1\to p_2\)

The claim is true.

For fixed \(y\ge 2\), we can use the finite-sum representation

\[
f_Y(y;p_1,p_2)
=
p_1p_2
\sum_{k=0}^{y-2}
(1-p_1)^k(1-p_2)^{y-2-k}.
\]

This expression is a finite sum of products of continuous functions of \((p_1,p_2)\). Therefore it is continuous jointly in \((p_1,p_2)\). In particular, it is continuous as \(p_1\to p_2\).

Equivalently, if \(p_2=p\) is fixed and \(p_1\to p\), then for \(y\ge 2\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{p_1\to p}
\frac{p_1p}{p-p_1}
\left\{(1-p_1)^{y-1}-(1-p)^{y-1}\right\}
&=
p^2 (y-1)(1-p)^{y-2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

This is exactly the value of the pmf when \(p_1=p_2=p\). For \(y=1\), the pmf is identically \(0\), so continuity is immediate.

Hence

\[
\boxed{
\text{For every fixed } y\in\{1,2,\dots\},\ f_Y(y;p_1,p_2)
\text{ is continuous as } p_1\to p_2.
}
\]
